headline: August Heat Sends Saybrook Stripers into the Dark Hours
subhead: With the shad run six weeks gone and river water pushing into the mid-70s, the bass have gone nocturnal while bluefish and snappers own the daylight.
body_markdown:
The silversides are running thick along the Great Island flats now — you can see them balling up against the marsh banks at low light, little flashes of nervous water that tell you everything about where the predators are staying. That's the real calendar down here in August. Forget the tide chart for a minute. When the silversides bunch up tight like that, with terns working them from above and something pushing from below, you know the river's settled into its dog-days rhythm. I've watched this happen every August for fifty years and it never gets old, even when the fishing itself gets stubborn.

And it has gotten stubborn, if I'm honest with you. The shad are long gone — pushed out to sea back in May, the hickories right behind them — and what we're left with for the next six weeks is a striped bass fishery that's decided daylight isn't worth the trouble. Water temps in the lower river and out toward the Sound have been sitting in that mid-to-upper 60s to low 70s range, warm enough that the bass have shifted hard nocturnal. I talked to a guy at the DEP Marina ramp last Tuesday morning who'd fished the outgoing tide from 4 AM to sunrise off Saybrook Point and had three fish in the mid-20s to keep him honest, all on live eels drifted along the breakwater rocks. By 7 AM, with the sun up and the water flat calm, it was over. Nothing. That's the pattern right now — a tight window either side of first light and last light, and dead water in between.

If you want stripers, plan around that clock. The river mouth itself — that stretch from the outer breakwater at Saybrook Point up through the mouth channel — is holding fish around the bunker schools that have pushed in with the warm water. Chunk bunker on a fish-finder rig, fished tight to bottom on the last two hours of the outgoing, has been the most consistent producer after dark. If you're throwing plugs, work the eddies off the rock jetties at Saybrook Point right at first light with a black Danny-style swimmer or a bone SP Minnow — slow, twitchy retrieve, right in that seam where the current breaks off the rocks. North Cove in Old Lyme has given up a few fish the same way, right at dawn before the powerboat traffic stirs the cove up.

Bluefish are the ones actually earning their keep in daylight right now, and that tracks with what's happening up and down the whole Sound this summer — warm surface water, bait pushed shallow, and blues more than happy to feed hard in conditions that put stripers off. Snapper blues have moved into the marina basins and along the Essex town dock in good numbers, which is a nice thing to hand a kid with a bobber and a strip of squid — they're maybe 6 to 9 inches now, aggressive, and they'll keep a rod bent all afternoon if you're patient. The adult bluefish, 3 to 6 pounds, have been working the Great Island flats and the mouth of the Lieutenant River on incoming water, chopping up the same silverside schools the terns are keying on. Small metal — half-ounce Deadly Dicks or Kastmasters — cast into the surface action and retrieved fast has been the ticket. Don't overthink the blues right now. They're not subtle.

White perch, if you're looking for something to fill a slower afternoon, are still holding in the deeper holes up around Essex and above — 12 to 18 feet, soft mud bottom, right where the river narrows a bit. Small jigs tipped with bloodworm or a sliver of bunker, fished slow near bottom on a dropping tide, will still take a limit of perch in the 8 to 10 inch range most days. It's not glamorous fishing but it's about as sure a thing as this river offers in August, and it gets you out on the water when the striper bite has shut down for the day.

We're building toward a new moon over the next several days, and that's going to put more push into these tides than we've had — worth watching, because a stronger current through the mouth and along Great Island usually pulls more bait through and can extend that dawn window a little longer than usual. If I had one morning to fish this week, I'd be at Saybrook Point breakwater working the last hour of dark into first light on the building tide, eel or plug, and I'd have bunker chunks rigged as backup once the sun came up in case the bass had already slid off. It won't be easy fishing. It rarely is in the first week of August on this river. But the bones of a good bite are there if you're willing to keep banker's hours in reverse.
